However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, pose, and shape from a single viewpoint image, showcasing the practical applications of our model in areas such as radiography and visible-light to near-infrared image matching.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed.

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron point distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass.

Precise and rapid flow velocity predictions of meandering rivers are crucial, 
especially when assessing flow dynamics and sediment transport.  Advanced 
traditional numerical models though, may overlook the complexities introduced 
to these systems by laser flumes.  This study explores a diverse range of 
machine learning models to develop predictors capable of accurately capturing 
flow velocities in the laboratory.  By utilizing two distinct datasets, we 
evaluated various models' abilities to forecast flow velocities in the 
laboratory, with support vector regression and artificial neural networks 
proving particularly effective.  These flow velocity prediction tools are now 
being integrated into a comprehensive laboratory framework that also includes 
sediment transport models, paving the way for more efficient river flow model 
upgrades.  Notably, we found that replacing the traditional models' near-bank 
velocity predictions with more accurate measurements resulted in improved 
accuracy of the laboratory model's bed elevation predictions.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach and outperforming another common algorithm in both
quantitative and qualitative assessments. The source code is freely available on
GitHub.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution and optimal temperature management within catalytic fixed bed reactors is vital for their reliable operation and optimal performance. A theoretical framework has been developed to determine optimal temperature distribution in such reactors, focusing on the conversion of reactants in their outflow. The framework was first analyzed for reactors without heat losses, and subsequent examination considered heat losses, leading to a practical application of the theory. In this application, the optimal temperature profile in a methane conversion reactor was determined, with comparison made to the temperature distribution observed in an experimentally operated reactor.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual simulation of left ventricular contraction and relaxation.

The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, along with the non-crossing pair-partitions that relate to its second-order moments, have been extensively studied in various contexts. A broader extension of this concept, known as non-pattern partitions, has recently emerged in the fields of probability theory and combinatorics, with implications for random matrix theory and possible connections to universal behavior in large random matrices. This paper seeks to explore the behavior of a class of limiting spectral measures defined by specific polynomial ensembles, focusing on those possessing joint probability densities characterized by non-pattern partitions. By analyzing these distributions, the authors investigate the distribution of external eigenvalues in the limit, showing that they converge to discrete support comprising distinct value clusters.

Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, the field of AI-powered video creation has gained momentum. This field is unique due to its interdisciplinary nature, which presents a significant hurdle for researchers who are new to the subject. A current void exists in comprehensive surveys on AI-powered video creation, which is an area we aim to address through a thorough review of applicable AI techniques and the development of a taxonomy that breaks down the process into three distinct phases. This taxonomy includes visual material extraction, storyline development, and post-production enhancements to optimize viewing experience. We will also discuss the most commonly employed evaluation metrics, associated datasets, emerging trends, and key challenges within this area, with a focus on the role of AI in promoting causes and influencing consumer behavior through the creation of persuasive video content.

Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations.

Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, a functional microacoustic metagrating prototype was created and experimentally demonstrated to efficiently redirect an incident plane wave with over 90% transmission.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing both bounded and unbounded control systems. The discussion focuses on systems that can be described by the differential inclusion $\dot{x} = f(x) + g(u)$, where the set-valued map $g(u)$ is upper semi-continuous, with compact, convex, and non-empty images. A key contribution of this research is the identification of sufficient and necessary conditions for global asymptotic controllability and stabilizability in terms of control Lyapunov functions, which can be efficiently computed using a specific feedback law. The proposed method for achieving stabilizability results in the existence of a bounded, Lipschitz-continuous feedback control that ensures the closed-loop system's trajectories converge to the origin. This finding represents an extension of previously established results for smooth control systems and systems with bounded controls. The proofs of the proposed conditions for global asymptotic controllability and stabilizability in this research build upon foundational work in control Lyapunov functions and feedback stabilization techniques in control systems theory.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a single category, it can result in overly confident predictions. To address this challenge, our research proposes an innovative open-world softmaX (OX) formulation that accounts for the possibility of classes extending beyond the model's current knowledge. By modeling each class within its respective decision boundary, OX can capture not only separable classes but also clusters of outliers. To train this new approach, a new generalized cross-entropy loss has been developed to minimize the most confident class's score within its corresponding boundary. Our model demonstrates remarkable calibration performance, surpassing current leading methods on widely used benchmark datasets like CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, particularly when confronted with unfamiliar data or over-trained models.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails left by process executions. These methods aim to reconstruct processes, but their effectiveness is limited without considering the processes' underlying structures. Processes typically consist of typical patterns and exceptions. This study proposes using exception-based, exception-prone, and normal process classifications to enhance process discovery methods. Event data is analyzed to create three distinct process models and suggests an aggregation approach to identify exception triggers in processes. Lastly, this approach's validity is examined through an example process data set.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. However, Liger's data complexity necessitates a customized data processing system to refine its output in real-time, making it compatible with science-oriented data presentation tools. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. We have established a prototype of this data processing system and defined the communication interface with the relevant software systems at the observatory.

Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for the investigation of complex dynamics, specifically a chaotic mixture of oscillation patterns. Using numerical simulations, we develop two computational methods to identify this chaotic behaviour. Additionally, we examine how the system's dynamics evolve, alternately entering two distinct dynamical states, and attempt to predict these shifts. We also construct a mathematical framework to understand the emergence of mixed-mode oscillations through interactions at the ecosystem's limit cycle boundaries, filling a gap in existing literature that lacked such comprehensive analysis.

Determining whether bulge growth, or "inside-out" or "outside-in" galaxy formation, occurred, astronomers are investigating the connection between star formation rates (SFR) and structural parameters of galaxies. Utilizing a comprehensive database, the research team analyzed the relationship between galaxies' star formation rates and their morphological indices, including the Sersic index, by examining various subsets of galaxies. The studies revealed a consistent relationship between galaxies' star formation rates and their morphological indices, with more irregular galaxies exhibiting higher star formation rates, regardless of their Hubble sequence. Notably, a distinct subsequence of "blue" or "red" galaxies was found to influence the observed trends. When controlling for color, however, the relationship became weaker. A significant correlation was also found between galaxies' star formation rates and their morphological indices, with a correlation coefficient of 0.29. A higher correlation was observed in the case of a specific subset of "green" disk galaxies, with a correlation coefficient of 0.42. The research suggests that a significant correlation between galaxies' morphological indices and their star formation rates might serve as a useful gauge of "inside-out" or "outside-in" galaxy formation, while the lack of such a correlation in the overall sample of galaxies reflects the diverse pathways of galaxy formation, including mergers, and the effects of galaxies' morphological indices on their star formation rates.

This paper conducts sentiment analysis across languages, focusing on large datasets available online. It explores the challenges associated with analyzing vast amounts of user-generated content available online. Without requiring significant manual work to label data for purposes like classification, clustering, or evaluation, the paper discusses various methods for performing sentiment analysis without labeled data. It examines the advantages and limitations of each method and discusses the underlying issues with many existing techniques. The paper also investigates the problems arising from using multilingual models, including the issues with models trained on multiple languages and the difficulties with translating models trained on one language to others. The analysis covers the issues with evaluating the sentiment of comments or posts in various languages. It discusses the problems arising from the use of the adjectives to determine the sentiment of comments or posts in various languages. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. In addition, we outline the role of fence insertions in managing program coherence and validate our approach and analysis principles through applications and an performance optimization case study, which we implement and simulate to demonstrate the effectiveness of optimized fence placement.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, each of size k, from the natural numbers have a sumset with a size less than 6k, their union is contained within a broader subset with a significantly narrower difference than 6k. G. Kohayakawa and W. Lawronn investigated the random version of this theorem by examining the natural numbers subsets that are randomly selected and replaced with a specific graph G(n,p). In doing so, they found a threshold curve of p=n^{-1/2} and investigated the behavior of these subsets both to the left and to the right of this curve. Notably, they discovered that for a particular small sumset condition, almost all subsets of a random graph satisfy this condition and therefore, could apply the theorem to these subsets. Additionally, an important application of this research was used to establish a logarithmic anti-Ramsey number for a specific diagonal graph.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure's density for $(B^{H}+f)$, particularly proving that if the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of $f$ exceeds $H$ then the density function is a square-integrable function, or if $A$ has a non-empty interior and the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of $f$ is at least $H$ then almost everywhere the density function equals $1$, both cases leading to the desired results.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information for patients who may suffer from severe COVID-19 symptoms that are not easily explained. This paper operates on the assumption that these features have a meaningful context underlying them. By leveraging data augmentation techniques informed by the underlying distribution of these images, a simpler model is presented that can effectively utilise this information to make accurate predictions. This approach employs an energy-based model known as Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) to augment the images and allow the prediction model to learn the informative patterns. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated by outperforming the current best solution in terms of performance, while requiring a significantly lower computational cost to implement, while also revealing that the model can identify key aspects that may indicate a higher risk of severe symptoms in COVID-19 patients.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. In order to gain a deeper understanding, we created an annotated dataset with over 800 difficult proposals and identified the primary challenge as object localization. Various lightweight fair sampling methods were explored, with our method, Frequency-Aware Proposal Sampling (FAPS), exhibiting superior performance compared to other methods. We compared our approach on the Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) and COCO key object detection tasks, demonstrating that FAPS outperforms random sampling, proposal-centric RetNet, and produces more balanced proposal distributions while maintaining comparable performance, leading to improved detection of low-frequency difficult proposals.

This study offers a supervised action recognition solution that's effective even in the absence of light. We've obtained promising results by testing our approach on the ARID dataset, a significantly smaller and darker collection of video data. Notably, previous action recognition methods typically relied on well-lit datasets such as Kinetics and HMDB51. Our results indicate that our technique achieves remarkable accuracy despite being trained on a much reduced and poorly lit dataset of video sequences. Experiments on the ARID and NightActions datasets have yielded positive outcomes. We've also analyzed key elements that affect the performance of our model, including color space, brightness augmentation, and data interpolation.

This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' growth, characterized by the disk's lack of central supermassive black holes, which are actively forming stars. This, in turn, is attributed to the massive galaxies' irregularity, which suppresses star formation in their central regions through a high, lopsided $J_2$ amplitude. Furthermore, this research suggests a potential explanation for the observed, massive, disk-like $[\rm II] \lambda \lambda 6548, 6550$ in the galaxy's spectrum, which is often associated with hidden supermassive black holes. We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1710.01290. The revision is necessary due to newly acquired experimental data on resonance and non-resonance processes and an upgrade in the performance of the Daya Bay neutrino collaboration's detector. Under the UTZ framework, where minimal assumptions are incorporated, we derive several significant outcomes. First, we find that a leptonic Dirac $CP$-violating phase is physically significant, with a preference for its value to be close to $\pi$, and this could potentially be verified through upcoming neutrino experiments. Additionally, under certain conditions, the UTZ model can satisfy the observed value of $\theta_{ATM}$ without requiring any zero entries. Furthermore, UTZ enables us to derive straightforward, zero-entry texture relations that can be utilized to determine unknown parameters and validate the model's validity. Moreover, we confirm that radiative corrections do not substantially impact the model's zero-entry texture relations and zero-correlation predictions, and we discuss how these findings can be applied to resonance and non-resonance processes and scattering off neutrino beams.

We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 5 or greater. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is zero, specifically in instances when it does not equal zero.

Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code production and matching actual code structure.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze the interaction between gravitational waves and fluids.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced detection methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams.

A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption.

We have developed a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. It can predict real-world observations and outcomes in scenarios involving linear channel loss, including the associated gain levels, error rates in different measurement bases, and final key rates. Our model is versatile and can be applied to various MDI-QKD implementations that employ convex source states or diverse coding techniques. As such, it is an invaluable resource for analyzing and evaluating the performance of different MDI-QKD protocols.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, on a specific class of graph classes that use Baker's approach. The definition of this new class builds upon previous work by Baker and Baker, ensuring that each graph in it allows for a PTAS solution.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative for approximating the transport term. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent probabilistic processes whose generating paths can be deterministically determined.

Recent analyses of lepton flavor universality (LFU) violating decays have suggested that new physics beyond the Standard Model might exist, potentially influencing multiple areas. To gain insights into these potential effects, we have explored their implications on the decays of $B_c$ mesons into charmed mesons and gluons. By making assumptions based on color and helicity arguments, we have derived modifications to the LFU ratios caused by new physics in the form of a flavor changing $bb \to cc$ penguin operator. These changes are then related to $B_c$ meson decay constants through matrix elements, which in turn provide a theoretical prediction for the ratios of branching fraction and leptonic momentum spectrum. Our findings indicate that any variation in the LFU ratios observed in two-body decays of $B_c$ mesons into charmed mesons and light leptons can be interpreted as a sign of the same new physics that is currently under investigation.

Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical human-life dependent tasks demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the field of transparent neural networks, many proposed models fail to provide a comprehensive view of the network's inner structure. In this research, we've developed a novel transparent CNN framework, incorporating an interpretable component that offers a visually appealing representation of the input data. This component not only presents a heat map highlighting key input regions, but also offers a seemingly 3D view of the data, enabling a more nuanced understanding of the network's internal operations, an area previously unexplored in transparent neural networks research.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267666's core is found to be rotating much slower than its outer layers, with a significant difference in angular velocity. This apparent discrepancy can be explained by a unique interaction between the outer convection zone and the stellar outer shell, as predicted by computational models. The findings hold the key to understanding how evolution influences a star's internal dynamics, including its core's rotation rate, and could have implications for predicting the formation of planet formation remnants, such as white dwarfs with specific characteristics, following their progenitor's collapse.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms, posing risks to security and stability, particularly when verified facts are lacking on breaking news stories.  Due to the limited success of current fake news detection methods dealing with emerging events, it is crucial to identify more effective approaches to identify false information on new stories that have not been encountered before.  Analysis of existing methods reveals their inability to accurately detect fake news on emerging events, thereby underscoring the need for novel, unsupervised techniques capable of identifying false information on social media without prior labeling.  In this paper, we propose a new, unsupervised fake news detection framework called Frame-work dealing with Emerging Events (F3) Event Detector, which focuses on identifying false information on breaking news without requiring labeling.  Through detailed examination of top algorithms used to enhance relevance in search engines and information retrieval in multidimensional environments, we have designed an iterative multi-stage technique consisting of three main stages: feature learning, retrieval enhancement, and feedback refinement.  In the first stage, we extract and analyze a wide range of features from social media data, user interactions, and network structures, thereby learning optimized representations in a self-reinforcing manner.  In the second stage, we enhance the precision of related information retrieval by employing cross-domain retrieval with optimal control and iterative multi-path attention algorithms.  In the final stage, we refine the quality of user-generated content by identifying and eliminating malicious influences, fake accounts, and spam interactions in an adaptive manner

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and initial condition $u(0,\cdot)\in L^{2}(S)$. The study aims to analyze the temporal evolution of solutions to this equation, as well as establish global solution existence, potential steady-states, and convergence rates to equilibrium, considering various values of $\kappa$ and $\lambda$.

This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras share in terms of quasi-bialgebras and twists. By establishing that set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions produce the same specific types of algebras and by identifying additional constraints for their 'q-deformed' counterparts, this research greatly expands our current understanding of set-theoretic solutions and their quantum equivalents, revealing new general patterns in the field.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in <110> silicon while utilizing <100> polarization.
The robust model developed allows the prediction of exchange interaction for any configuration of positions, orientations and valley coherence in <100> silicon.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm – and demonstrated their capability to accurately capture both its efficient inference performance and potential pitfalls. Notably, our model achieved a crucial insight that the graphical model structure is not solely responsible for the network's behavior, leading to the development of strategies to minimize generalization errors. Effectively, this allows the trained network to minimize loss functions on previously unseen graphs, with practical implications across various domains.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. It was also shown that they have strong quantum nonlocality, answering open questions from Halder and others, and providing a connection between this phenomenon and UPBs. To operationally demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality, a new task was also proposed.

The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to apply analyses systematically. However, current GP 2 specifications include only a limited set of rooted rules, which restricts their versatility. In this study, we propose an enhanced GP 2 framework that incorporates expanded sets of non-rooted rules, providing an efficient method to represent complex, parameterized program properties. We have developed GP 2 specifications that utilize these expanded sets of rules to solve key problems, such as determining reachability in systems with nested communications and calculating post-states for nested sessions in a protocol. Furthermore, we have developed a GP 2 solver that derives program properties by means of graph reachability calculations, and we have its correctness ensured by reducing it to standard model checking. We have demonstrated the framework's effectiveness by nested session protocol property analysis with the new solver.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique achieve significant performance gains over traditional models, including a notable increase in English vocabulary understanding within scientific knowledge graphs and enhanced reasoning capabilities when integrating new information, showcasing the potential benefit of structured information over natural language text.

This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. The article compares their solutions with classical PDE models under specific localization limits, as well as how rescaled fractional kernels relate to inhomogeneous fractional boundary value problems. These discussions shed light on the challenges and issues that arise in nonlocal problems with inhomogeneous data within bounded domains.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope to conduct a deep integral field unit (IFU) spectroscopy study on ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located in the local universe, as part of a broader survey called Super-KOOLS. This study employed a novel approach combining optical and sub-millimeter IFU data to reveal the physical characteristics of star-forming galaxies at various stages of merging. Our analysis revealed a notable trend in [OIII] outflow strength, where a significant increase from 1000 pc to >10 kpc occurs as galaxies progress from an early to a later merging stage. This increase is linked to an even more dramatic rise in gas turbulence velocity in the same merging stage. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the rise in turbulence velocity may be attributed to a corresponding increase in the mass outflow rate of metal ions per unit of star formation, which is particularly evident in the later merging stage. This research contributes to our understanding of the relationship between merging activity, galaxy evolution, and the regulation of growth through the ejection of metal-rich gas.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, the tangent hyperbolic function is utilized to develop a novel, non-convex type multivariate interpolation called the 'multiquadric-tanh' (MQ-tanh) interpolation. The proposed quadratic function-based approximation enables us to demonstrate the differentiability of the resulting interpolation function, along with its derivative properties. Notably, the convergence of the novel interpolation is shown to be analogous to that of the multiquadric, with key differences being a reduction in computational cost and preservation of non-convexity. Furthermore, the novel interpolation function exhibits enhanced stability, exhibiting resistance to oscillations and the creation of local extrema when interpolating a set of scattered data points. To validate the novel interpolation's efficiency and robustness, numerical experiments and comparative analyses with other multivariate interpolation methods are provided, along with the development of a novel sparse grid algorithm to address computational challenges arising from a large number of data points.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using tools like cameras and LiDAR sensors,
leverage image classification to identify specific weather states such as rain, snow,
and fog. However, these approaches are limited to basic weather states and do not
take into consideration weather intensity. In response to this shortcoming, we present
the RFS Dataset and associated algorithms aimed at identifying real-time weather states,
including low, medium, and high intensity categories for fog, rain, and snow.
The RFS Dataset contains meticulously labeled data, collected from the inside of vehicles
equipped with LiDAR sensors, and includes images of the driving environment as well as LiDAR point clouds.
It encompasses all weather conditions from perfect visibility to snow storms.
In addition to RFS Dataset release, we present baseline algorithms for weather state
detection using images, showing the effectiveness of our approach by comparing the results
to the human annotators' accuracy.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch and in the distant past, we find distinct distributions of turn-around radii that may serve as a distinguishing factor between these cosmologies, particularly when observed in large-scale surveys like Euclid, DESI, and WFIRST. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's sensitivity to present-day halo properties and how it can help identify the degeneracy of the $\Omega_{\rm m}-\log h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns.

A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on the SU(2) glueball spectrum for specific quantum numbers and at varying lattice spacings. The study employs published data to determine the spectral density and the glueball spectrum. The results for the ground state mass are consistent with the conventional approach using exponential correlations. Additionally, preliminary indications of excited states within the spectrum can be derived from the spectral density.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing chatbots that can engage in natural human-like conversations
while adhering to key requirements like maintaining a specific persona or avoiding
inappropriate content remains a major challenge.
The task's difficulty is compounded by the need to balance conflicting objectives
and the absence of sufficient, high-quality dialogue data that features such personae.
To address these issues, this study explores the problem of persona-based open-domain
dialogue systems and outlines its applications, data problems, model architectures,
evaluation metrics, and future research directions.
We identify limitations in current approaches and potential applications in
natural language processing and artificial intelligence, as well as insights for
improving existing systems and setting new industry standards.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting a sufficient number of observations for statistically meaningful results. Since experiments typically involve few treatment replications, conventional results are hard to interpret. To overcome this challenge, a novel framework has been developed using Bayesian analysis, shrinking variance estimates and efficiency rankings based on limited observation counts. This new framework is illustrated with a case study examining the efficacy of different pesticide treatments to control Japanese apple tree mites, where Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations are employed to calculate efficiency rankings and provide practical guidance on the most beneficial treatment options considering cost and variance uncertainty.

360-degree streaming videos are gaining popularity in areas like gaming and virtual tourism. To offer a unique tourism experience, users must download a 360-degree video that is larger in size compared to standard videos, which may cause issues for users with limited devices and internet connections. As an alternative, a 180-degree video tile can be projected onto the remaining 180-degree video sphere to enhance user experience while reducing the video size. Although this technique improves the viewing experience, it leaves a noticeable discontinuity in the 90-degree diagonal of the view. In contrast, a cutting surface can be used to divide the 360-degree video, which not only enhances the viewing experience but also has implications for texture mapping, video compression, and playback performance.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applicability of these constructed objects through a discussion on their employment in numerical tensor network algorithms.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces.

In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the L^p norm, applicable to any bounded area in R^n with smooth borders.
As a result, we derive inequalities including an anisotropic Willmore inequality, a sharp anisotropic Minkowski inequality, and a sharp volumetric anisotropic Minkowski inequality. Our proof involves a novel approach in nonlinear potential theory recently described in the reference provided.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies.
